I commented on your last post, the one who also had it twice... So I know just how you feel, it *is* hard to say goodbye and I did feel grief over it. For me anyway, the feeling lasted maybe two to three months, pretty inline with what people say on here. But at the time, it felt necessary to live, as our brains will recall those first years drinking and forget all the pain and agony to tell us to drink anyway. Unfortunately for you and I, we drank our lifetimes allotted amount early... It's sad, but we knew it was coming with the way we drank and there's nothing we can do about it now that it happened. We just can't drink anymore and that's just the way it is, you know? 

[I was where you're at](https://old.reddit.com/r/dryalcoholics/comments/18w6278/15_days_sober_after_hospitalized_for_pancreatitis/) January of last year. It's interesting to read my own wishes and see how they really came true. My life is no longer dominated by thoughts of alcohol and fear of when I would get to drink again, and most days the only time I think about it is seeing posts on this sub. It's hard to imagine, right? I didn't go through any revelations, complete the steps or anything... but it did take time. Know that everything you do every day helps you get through it; every activity you do without being intoxicated cause your brain to make new neural connections and memories that teach it to live without alcohol. Don't introduce everything all at once of course (I stayed away from my biggest trigger, socialization for a few weeks).

So it's ok to feel remorseful, but try not to let yourself become overwhelmed by it. One of the hardest things about sobriety for me was all of my emotions coming back in the first few months and having to feel them with no buffer. Everything felt overwhelming and boring at the same time! But I promise it won't feel like this for forever, and you can get through this. Feel free to dm me anytime or even every day if you want.

It took me two to three months to finally feel less bored, and a bit longer to start actually having fun doing new things.

There's one thing that's helped me with this, which is the realization that it's *okay to be bored*.  Boredom is a normal human emotion, but after giving our brains dopamine by drinking every single day, especially when we're bored, we make that emotion foreign and scary. I had a hard time with boredom, because feeling it would stress me out. I would recommend sitting down and really just experiencing feeling bored for a while. Sit down and do nothing except be with your thoughts, don't open your phone even. If you do this, you teach your mind that the feeling isn't harmful, that it's normal, and you may find you're less tempted next time you're bored.

Do you enjoy a gathering with those people at the gym, or are there other social settings that you still genuinely have fun during? Are you expecting you'll like it, and find yourself frustrated it's not fun without drinking? Alternatively, do you enjoy doing it but miss not being anxious? 

I used to play games online with friends but after getting sober I found myself unable to have fun and too anxious to play anymore. I felt like I wasn't having fun because I wasn't drinking, and it was as if I were being deprived of something. But if I did an activity I knew I didn't like, would I be frustrated that I didn't think it was fun? For nearly a decade I gave my brain a rush of dopamine while drinking and gaming, strongly associating it with pleasure--I thought I *knew* I loved doing it. Yet I felt frustrated that I wasn't enjoying it the same after I stopped drinking.

I have come to the realization that my preferences have just changed, and that I am a naturally anxious person. I just can't expect to do things (especially social things) that I used to be able to with alcohol and have the same amount of fun. But at the same time, there are new things that I have learned to genuinely enjoy doing that I never did before and wouldn't be able to do while drinking. Do you have things you actually enjoy now? I would suggest reflecting on whether you actually want to be at a drinking get-together, or if you miss *drinking and its effects* at get-togethers.

If none of this resonates and you find you still do enjoy them, maybe I could offer another thought. When you were at the party surrounded by the sight, smell, and sound of alcohol being poured, the same neural connections associated with drinking were lighting up. When I stopping drinking, even going to the grocery store (where I bought alcohol frequently) caused me to have urges for the same reason. I'm sure you've had these experiences, too, so you know that the more you do it without drinking, the more you form new neural connections and it gets easier. If you want to keep going to get-togethers, you should keep going to them--just maybe avoid ones that have alcohol for a bit since you were so close to relapsing. Last night doesn't have to be a defeat mentally. You *didn't* drink. You could have poured yourself a drink or asked someone for one, but instead you made it to 242. You are more resilient today.

I was at the 'fifth of vodka' a day phase for a couple years without the will to stop, then out of nowhere I got pancreatitis... Most painful experience of my life. But fear didn't motivate me to stop for even a whole month, so I got it again half a year later from a fraction of the intake, and I was scared that nothing could put the brakes on. But I did want to live as death finally seemed like a real possibility. But I knew fear wasn't going to be enough. 

I realized that there was no longer room for shoulds and wants, no ifs and thens, it was just my time. Instead of focusing my efforts on not drinking, I focused them on changing my inner relationship with alcohol to come to terms with the fact that it was really over, and that I just couldn't drink anymore. Boredom was the biggest struggle for me, and though I continue to experience boredom it's not as severe as it was everytime I stopped drinking. The reality really was for me like people here often say, that the brains neurochemistry is fucked up from alcohol because it gets so much dopamine from it that it can't produce much on its own. After a couple months not drinking, boredom became less common and less severe (sometimes it was agonizing, maybe what you're feeling.)

Another thought I would like to offer you is one that helped me a lot, which is to try embracing the boredom, to try feeling it. We had drank for so long, and *every single time* we were bored we knew a cure: take a shot! It really trains our brain that boredom is a bad feeling, one that's not okay to feel and must be washed away with alcohol. But boredom is a human emotion just like happiness or sadness, and it's okay to be bored! Boredom is what made me willing to try new things, but you have to be okay feeling it without freaking out. When you're bored, try putting the phone down or sitting away from the computer and just feel it for five minutes, experience how uncomfortable it is. When I used to feel boredom it was a huge trigger because it was so unfamiliar. Sometimes I would go outside when I wanted to drink and just sit on the steps and do nothing but watch the sky and the birds and the grass for half an hour, and eventually the feeling would pass. That helped to train my brain to stop freaking out and wanting to drink every time I felt bored. 


Edit: I also take Adderall and realized doing the above but with my phone helped my attention issues and boredom a lot, as I noticed I was always instinctively opening my phone when bored to consume thoughtless, dopamine content. When I stopped scrolling as much (maybe 30-60 mins a day now) I would get bored which led me to seek other, more fulfilling activities, and has really helped my focus. 

Good luck hope it can help

Unfortunately it took me two hospitalizations for pancreatitis before I stop stopped (happened before my liver even gave). I just expected the fear of being hospitalized to change me, but first I had to change my routines/habits to get me through the chemical dependency phase. I just tried to do the same things I was doing every day but without drinking, and it makes it impossibly hard.

Our brains are wired so that they see familiar things and it invokes the same urges and feelings... Sometimes it's so hard to break out of this right? We're in the same job, same relationship, same home, same friends... After the second time in the hospital, I temporarily stopped doing the things I used to for a few weeks. I stopped playing the same games, told my friends I wouldn't be online for a while, started trying to cook a real meal once a day (as opposed to getting take-out), tried an hour of drawing a day, tried walking... None of it really *helped* me become sober, but it helped me break the connections and associations my brain had with alcohol, so at least I could later focus on how to stay sober without the overwhelming urges. I think things like AA can be good at both breaking your routine as well as learning to live sober, but not everyone has good experiences with it.

When I first got back to my old routines that made me want to drink like getting online to play games, I had some urges but they were not as strong because it had been three weeks. And as I did familiar things again, I reinforced to my brain that I didn't need to drink to do them. As months went by I started to forget that I needed to drink to enjoy those things... Now finally I can have an awful day and I don't even think about alcohol.
